validator: draft 1 passes with no problems, soft points or warnings
keep: The idea is named up front: repeat readings pile up round a middle, and the middle and spread are what the reading is.

The picture is the brief's balancing pile: fifty simulated Zs readings of an example 0.80 Ω circuit read to 0.01 Ω, pegs as the twelve nudges, a fulcrum at the mean, the random error slider and the ringed bead as a slipped probe; the five-bead pile on the same beam for hand working.

Worked examples with real numbers from the rules: 4.05 ÷ 5 = 0.81 Ω with 0.04 Ω of distance each side; a 1.00 Ω slip in fifty lifts the mean 0.02 Ω; the SD of 0.77-0.82 Ω worked to 0.02 Ω with n − 1; 0.02 to about 0.14 Ω after the slip (checked over 2000 simulated batches: 0.13 to 0.15).

Each brief misconception has a puzzle with its own hint: range alone (screen 6), bar heights or bumpiness (screen 10), far apart rather than far from the mean (screen 6's piled-at-the-ends B), the recipe without the readings (screens 12 and 13 ask what the number says), forgetting the root (screen 8's 0.0009), and which kind of mean (screens 11 and 13).
Thirteen screens alternate SHOW (1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11) and DO (2, 4, 6, 8, 10), ending with two mixed puzzles (12, 13).
Two footnotes, each on a rule he might look up; n − 1 is put as 'textbooks add', unfootnoted, since no kept source states it. No source is named in the text.
The analogy is from his trade: DC level and ripple, the SD as the RMS of the ripple, with the n − 1 difference in breaks.
fix: Causal step skipped: why halving the random error halves the width and nearly doubles the height. Say each reading's distance from the true value is the error times its nudges, so halving the error halves every distance, and the same fifty beads crowd into about half as many columns. 'Nearly' because the meter's 0.01 Ω step rounds them.
Causal step skipped: why the median moves one place at most. Say every other reading keeps its place, so only one reading crosses the middle.
Causal step skipped: why the slip lifts the SD so far. Say its squared distance, about 1, dwarfs the other forty-nine's total of about 0.02.
False absolute: 'it balances at the same point' after halving. The batch mean is the true value plus the error times the mean nudge, so it moves very slightly. Say 'in very nearly the same place'.

False absolute that a later idea breaks: 'Ten repeat readings of one circuit give that circuit's value'. Lesson 2 shows a meter offset that repeating cannot remove. Say they tell you about that one circuit.
Qualifier: the spread of ten different circuits is 'mostly how the circuits differ' only when they differ by more than the reading wobbles. Say it plainly, 'plus a little wobble'.
Analogy: ripple is not always a smooth wave (a rectifier's is a sawtooth). Say it repeats in a set pattern.
Misconception not named in explain: a bumpy pile is not more spread than a smooth one. Add one sentence.

Brief shows the effect but the cause needs to be on screen too: on screen 5 each bead's jinks through the pegs shrink to half. Add to whatAmILookingAt, and name the median's tick under the beam that screen 3 watches.
Plain writing: paragraph 3 runs to over 250 words and two sentences pass 24 words. Split the paragraph at the range, and split the long sentences.
Practice: 'usually the key marked s or σn−1' becomes 'often', since keys differ by make.
